title: Doppelgängers

jokes.text: Things are exactly the way they were back in 1817, except, you know, women and minorities can vote, we have indoor toilets, and we no longer burn widows for learning arithmetic.
jokes.setup: Official frames the merger as a historic return to 1817 roots, evoking nostalgia
jokes.punchline: Escalating list of horrific 1817 practices — ending on the absurdly specific 'burn widows for learning arithmetic' — undercuts the nostalgia completely
jokes.explanation: The joke builds with perfect escalation — each item in the list is funnier and more specific than the last. 'Burn widows for learning arithmetic' is a brilliant comedic peak: absurdly specific, historically flavored, and completely unexpected. The structure earns its laughs through the rule of three with a dark kicker.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: In 1817, only white men could vote. Now anyone can vote. Progress!

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: In 1817, if your wife did your taxes wrong, you could burn her. Now you can't. So really, we've gone backwards.

jokes.text: There are two Eagleton departments Pawnee does not have: the Department of Infinity Pool Design and the Department of Dressage.
jokes.setup: Officials are mapping equivalent departments between the two cities
jokes.punchline: Eagleton's absurdly luxurious, frivolous government departments reveal the town's elitist excess
jokes.explanation: Sharp world-building joke that crystallizes Eagleton's character — their government funded infinity pool design as an official department. Economical and well-targeted satire of wealthy town excess.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: It's not horse-riding, it's horse-dancing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Horse-dancing?

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Yes. Horse-dancing.

jokes.text: ...which I am told is a fancy horse-riding thing. / It is horse-dancing, madam.
jokes.setup: Official dismissively describes dressage as 'a fancy horse-riding thing'
jokes.punchline: An Eagletonian solemnly corrects the official: 'It is horse-dancing, madam' — defending the dignity of horse-dancing with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes entirely from Alonzo's absolute deadpan sincerity. The correction 'It is horse-dancing, madam' is delivered with such wounded dignity that it becomes genuinely quotable. Perfect economy — four words do all the work. The pomposity of the correction is itself the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I would watch that.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: It's called dressage.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: No, I mean I would watch the meeting if everyone was treating it like they're on horses.

jokes.text: Okay, take it easy, Alonzo. All you horse dancing people, sit in your saddles if you will.
jokes.setup: Alonzo's correction about horse-dancing has presumably caused a stir among the dressage crowd
jokes.punchline: 'Sit in your saddles if you will' — the official addresses the horse-dancing contingent as a distinct political bloc with their own seating protocol
jokes.explanation: Quick callback that extends the horse-dancing absurdity. 'Sit in your saddles' is a perfectly absurd crowd-management phrase that treats dressage riders as though they are literally mounted during the meeting. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm one of a kind. I'm like those custom shoes they make in Italy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Except instead of being handcrafted by artisans, I was mass-produced in a factory, and instead of being worth thousands of dollars, I'm worth about forty bucks.

jokes.text: Attention: Eagleton is now under martial law. / No.
jokes.setup: A voice announces martial law — a wildly disproportionate governmental response
jokes.punchline: Ben's single flat 'No.' — the entire comedic weight rests on the absolute calm refusal
jokes.explanation: Maximum comedic economy — one word, perfectly placed. Ben's flat bureaucratic 'No.' to martial law is both in-character (the competent straight man) and structurally flawless. The gap between the absurdity of the announcement and the calmness of the refusal is the entire joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Good morning, everyone! It's a beautiful day!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh God, no. Why would you say that? You've doomed us all.

jokes.text: Guess there's no Tom Haverford equivalent. Not surprised, I'm one of a kind, just like the custom Nikes I designed that say 'Tommy's Tootsies' across the toes.
jokes.setup: Leslie notes there's no Tom Haverford equivalent among the Eagleton staff
jokes.punchline: Tom agrees he's 'one of a kind' and immediately proves his unique brand of narcissism by referencing his custom Nikes labeled 'Tommy's Tootsies'
jokes.explanation: 'Tommy's Tootsies' is a perfectly Tom-specific detail — the specific vanity of custom-labeling his own Nikes with a babyish nickname for his feet. Only Tom Haverford would do this and say it with pride. Strong character integration elevates what would otherwise be a standard narcissism joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, I have your new business cards.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh, great! Thanks, Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: They say 'Gerry Gergich, Parks Department.'

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: It's Jerry. Jerry Gergich.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Right, right. Well, the printer said they're non-refundable.

jokes.text: You do have a counterpart, actually. His name is Eric, and I've heard he's amazing.
jokes.setup: Tom has just bragged he's irreplaceable and one of a kind
jokes.punchline: Leslie casually reveals he does have a counterpart — and immediately delivers the twist knife: 'I've heard he's amazing'
jokes.explanation: Well-structured deflation of Tom's ego. The rewatch bonus comes from knowing Eric turns out to be a computer program, making Leslie's 'he's amazing' line even funnier in retrospect. Clean structure with good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: My name is actually Garry. G-A-R-R-Y.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh, so it's Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, he said Gary. G-A-R-Y.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: No, Garry. With two Rs.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Right, Larry.

jokes.text: Hey, everybody. / No! No, why? This can't be happening. Why, Leslie?
jokes.setup: Leslie announces a surprise — the staff anticipates something new
jokes.punchline: Jerry walks in and the entire office reacts with visceral despair — 'No! No, why?' — as though a villain has returned
jokes.explanation: The running gag of the office hating Jerry is well-executed here — the collective 'No!' reaction is disproportionately horrified for a filing temp returning. It's a strong reactivation of an established bit. Good character integration because this reaction could only happen in THIS office with THIS character.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: My wife doesn't even call me Jerry anymore. She just sighs and points at things.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's... that's actually kind of sad, Jerry.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: My name's not even Jerry.

jokes.text: And as long as we're starting out fresh, Leslie, I was wondering if people would call me by my real name. / Larry? / No, it's not Larry. It's Jerry. No, it's Gary. / Your name is Larry, Larry Gengurch.
jokes.setup: Jerry asks to be called by his real name on his return — a reasonable request
jokes.punchline: The name confusion escalates: he corrects 'Larry' to 'Jerry,' then second-guesses himself to 'Gary,' before Leslie and April firmly establish his name is 'Larry Gengurch' — he doesn't even know his own name at this point
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's best jokes. The escalation is perfect: Jerry's attempt to reclaim dignity immediately collapses into him not even knowing his own name. The bit works on multiple levels — the office's casual cruelty, Jerry's hapless defeat, and the absurd implication that years of name abuse have genuinely confused him about his identity. 'Your name is Larry, Larry Gengurch' delivered with total confidence is a standout line. Highly quotable and character-essential.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you're like America's founding father, except instead of fighting the British, you're fighting the government. Which is ironic because you work for the government.

jokes.text: April, Tom and Donna are three of the best human beings that have ever lived. Ron is basically a better version of George Washington. But...the Eagletonians are probably good too.
jokes.setup: Leslie is supposed to be objectively evaluating who to keep after the merger
jokes.punchline: She lavishes over-the-top praise on her Pawnee team ('better version of George Washington') then adds a completely unconvincing, deflated 'the Eagletonians are probably good too'
jokes.explanation: Very Leslie — her inability to pretend to be objective about her team is a core character trait. The contrast between 'better version of George Washington' and the mumbled afterthought about Eagletonians lands well. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We have a system. I motivate people with positive reinforcement and careful planning.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: And I fire people.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's a good system.

jokes.text: Today, we are not just merging two towns. We're throwing a birthday party for a new city. Happy birthday, New Pawnee.
jokes.setup: Leslie addresses the crowd about the merger
jokes.punchline: The grandiosity of 'throwing a birthday party for a new city' — and naming it 'New Pawnee' — is classic Leslie over-investment in civic ceremony
jokes.explanation: Competent Leslie character joke — the sentimentality and the self-important naming are both on-brand. Functional but not exceptional; the setup is a bit broad.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I came back because I realized I missed working here. Plus, Gayle in a bikini... let's just say it motivated me to get back in shape.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'm going to be a hero. A real hero. Like a fireman, but better.

jokes.text: Party's over. You guys lost millions of taxpayer dollars, and we have to clean up the obscene mess you've made.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just warmly welcomed everyone with birthday party framing
jokes.punchline: Ben immediately deflates the mood with blunt accountant reality — 'Party's over' is a perfect one-two with Leslie's preceding optimism
jokes.explanation: Juxtaposition between Leslie's birthday party framing and Ben's immediate 'party's over' is well-structured. Works as both a callback and a character contrast. The line 'obscene mess' has the right Ben-specific flavor.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh, a banana! I'll just keep this in my desk for a healthy snack later.

jokes.text: You're not as nice as the other guy.
jokes.setup: Ben has just curtly told the Eagletonians they lost millions and made an obscene mess
jokes.punchline: An Eagletonian's plaintive observation that Ben is 'not as nice as the other guy' — treating fiscal accountability as a matter of manners
jokes.explanation: Quick, clean line that characterizes Eagletonians as accustomed to being coddled. Good economy. The comedy comes from the entitled obliviousness of the complaint.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Donna! What a beautiful name! It's so strong, so powerful! Donna could be a warrior queen, or a successful businesswoman, or a dolphin trainer!

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: It's just a name, Craig.

jokes.text: When we were state auditors, we had an amazing system. Yeah, Chris pumped everyone up and made them feel positive and happy. And I swooped in and slashed their budgets to ribbons. / Like a majestic alley-oop.
jokes.setup: Ben describes their former auditing system as 'amazing'
jokes.punchline: Chris's athletic metaphor 'like a majestic alley-oop' for budget devastation — the collision of Chris's relentless positivity with the reality that he was the setup man for financial destruction
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. The 'majestic alley-oop' metaphor is perfectly Chris — athletic, uplifting language applied to a destructive process. The idea that Chris would frame being the human distraction for budget slashing as a beautiful sports play is deeply in character and conceptually original. 'Majestic' is the perfect modifier. Among the episode's top jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: My name is Craig. It's the most boring name in the world. You know what I wish my name was? Thunderbottom. Thunderbottom Silk Mane.

jokes.text: You're all amazing! / You're all fired. / Teamwork.
jokes.setup: Chris and Ben describe their old system; we see it enacted
jokes.punchline: The rapid-fire sequence — Chris pumps up, Ben fires everyone, Ben deadpans 'Teamwork' — compresses the alley-oop description into a perfect three-beat
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's structural comedy highlight. The three-word final beat 'Teamwork.' delivered deadpan by Ben after firing everyone is a masterclass in economy. It's a callback that pays off the alley-oop description immediately, with perfect timing compression. The structure is nearly flawless: setup (Chris), subversion (Ben), button (Ben's 'Teamwork'). Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I don't need a vacation. I need to be here, managing this office. Every day I come in and I give one hundred and ten percent. You know what that means? It means I'm overextended and probably gonna have a heart attack by fifty-two.

jokes.text: Hi, you've reached the voicemail of Larry Gengurch.
jokes.setup: We cut to a confessional that appears to be Jerry speaking about returning from retirement
jokes.punchline: The cut reveals Jerry's phone voicemail is playing — implying even the show can't be bothered to have Larry speak directly, or that Leslie called his voicemail instead of reaching him
jokes.explanation: An inventive structural joke — the confessional 'talking head' that turns out to be a voicemail message is a clever format subversion. It also uses 'Larry Gengurch' from the earlier name gag, rewarding attentive viewers. The economy is excellent; the joke is in the reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Tynnyfer
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Tynnyfer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's... an interesting spelling.

dialogue.speaker: Tynnyfer
dialogue.line: I know. I rebranded myself. I used to be Jennifer, but I added a 'Y' and two 'N's to make it more unique.

jokes.text: Well, when Leslie called to see if I could help, Gayle and I were just getting on a cruise ship to the Bahamas. I said, 'Gayle, put that bikini away, because Pawnee needs me.'
jokes.setup: Jerry describes being called out of retirement
jokes.punchline: The heroic framing ('Pawnee needs me') applied to being a filing temp — plus the specific domestic detail of commanding his wife to put away her bikini — transforms a sad situation into unearned grandiosity
jokes.explanation: Classic Jerry joke — he narrates his life with completely unearned heroic framing. The Gayle bikini detail is specific and funny. Competent character work; the sadness underlying the comedy is appropriate for this character.

dialogue.speaker: Tynnyfer
dialogue.line: Yeah, I take pills to wake up, pills to sleep, pills to stay focused during the day. My doctor says I'm doing great.

jokes.text: Oh ho! Somebody forgot a banana in here--ooh!
jokes.setup: Jerry's heroic voicemail message is playing — he's built himself up as answering Pawnee's call
jokes.punchline: Mid-voicemail, Jerry finds an old banana and injures himself — collapsing the heroic narrative with immediate, mundane physical comedy
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jerry beat — the pratfall during his own voicemail message is conceptually inspired. He hurts himself on a forgotten banana while attempting to sound heroic. The offscreen physical comedy is funnier for being entirely inferred. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh my gosh, you guys! This is so exciting! I am literally thrilled about everything right now! This project is going to be absolutely bonking amazing!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: And I just want to say, you all are doing such a bonking great job. Really, truly bonking fantastic work, everyone.

jokes.text: Hi, I'm Donna. / Oh, that is the perfect name for you. I love it. Never change it!
jokes.setup: Donna introduces herself to Craig
jokes.punchline: Craig's ecstatic, over-the-top response to literally just her name — 'that is the perfect name for you, I love it, never change it!' — is absurdly disproportionate
jokes.explanation: An excellent introduction to Craig's character — his intensity is immediately apparent from his reaction to a name. The joke lands because the response is so wildly disproportionate to the stimulus. Good first impression of a new character.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Tynnyfer is the worst. She's stupid, she's annoying, and she has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. I hate everything about her. Also, she has amazing hair and I think she's really cool and funny. But seriously, I can't stand her.

jokes.text: Ugh, yes, but I hate that name. It's so boring. Sounds like someone's cousin. Craig! Craig! I want to be a Spanish man named Terrence, but that didn't happen.
jokes.setup: Donna confirms he's Craig — a perfectly normal name
jokes.punchline: Craig's theatrical hatred of his own name, complete with the specific fantasy of being 'a Spanish man named Terrence' — a name that is not particularly Spanish
jokes.explanation: Genuinely original — the combination of Craig's intense self-hatred about a generic name, his theatrical repetition of 'Craig! Craig!', and the specific absurdist detail that he wants to be 'a Spanish man named Terrence' (which is not a particularly Spanish name) is brilliantly layered. The joke rewards attention. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Dunne? Like the name?

dialogue.speaker: Other Character
dialogue.line: Yes, why?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Sounds like you're done.

jokes.text: Oh, I did everything. Everything! I carried the Eagleton department on my shoulders for years, and I loved every second of it. You don't even know!
jokes.setup: Donna calmly lists her duties as office manager
jokes.punchline: Craig's dramatically over-the-top response — 'You don't even know!' — escalating his description of carrying the department to near-heroic martyrdom
jokes.explanation: Craig's volcanic intensity applied to basic job duties continues to establish his character effectively. 'You don't even know!' is the right button — it implies depths of suffering that don't exist.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I don't understand how these new phones work.

dialogue.speaker: Ragiv
dialogue.line: Tom, that phone came out three years ago.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Exactly. Ancient history.

dialogue.speaker: Ragiv
dialogue.line: You're wearing a Bluetooth headset from 2006.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This is vintage, Ragiv. Vintage is in.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, was your name Jennifer? / No, it's Tynnyffer with two y's. I used to be Jennifer, but then I decided to rebrand myself.
jokes.setup: April asks Tynnyfer her name
jokes.punchline: Tynnyfer explains she 'rebranded' herself from Jennifer — the corporate language applied to renaming oneself, plus the absurdity of two y's
jokes.explanation: Sharp satirical jab at a certain type of rebranded wellness-obsessed person. 'Rebrand myself' is the perfect word choice — treating personal identity like a marketing exercise. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You can see the shoulder pads? I thought they were subtle.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's the whole point of shoulder pads — nobody's supposed to notice them!

jokes.text: Oh, wait, hang on. It's Xanax o'clock.
jokes.setup: Tynnyfer is in the middle of explaining her rebranding
jokes.punchline: She casually interrupts herself mid-sentence to announce it's time for her Xanax as though it's a scheduled appointment — 'Xanax o'clock' normalizing pharmaceutical dependence with breezy lifestyle language
jokes.explanation: 'Xanax o'clock' is an excellent coinage — the casual wellness-culture framing of prescription drug dependency. The interruption mid-sentence makes it land even harder. Highly quotable and economical. Strong character detail for Tynnyfer.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Pawnee has the highest rate of spontaneous baldness in the entire country.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That doesn't sound right.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: We also have an epidemic of what we call 'Pawnee Fever.' Symptoms include fever, confusion, and the inability to tell the difference between a hot dog and a calzone.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I have that!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yes, you do, Jerry.

jokes.text: April complimenting Tynnyfer's dress as 'bonks' and faking enthusiasm — she immediately tells the camera 'She's the worst person I've ever met. I want to travel the world with her.'
jokes.setup: April has clearly identified Tynnyfer as everything she despises — bubbly, vapid, over-enthusiastic
jokes.punchline: April's confessional reveals the exact opposite: 'She's the worst person I've ever met. I want to travel the world with her.' — April's nihilism accidentally produces genuine connection
jokes.explanation: Among the episode's best jokes. The construction is perfect: April's self-image is built on hating enthusiastic people, but the punchline reveals she's been completely won over. 'She's the worst person I've ever met. I want to travel the world with her.' is a beautiful contradiction that tells us everything about April — and about Tynnyfer. Could only be April's line. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you are such a good friend, and you have really nice feet. Like, disproportionately nice feet. They're like little baby feet, but on an adult.

jokes.text: Last name? / Dunne. / Is that your name, or are you telling me you're finished talking? / Both. / Dunne and done.
jokes.setup: Pawnee Ron asks Eagleton Ron for his last name
jokes.punchline: Eagleton Ron's name is 'Dunne,' which sounds like 'done' — leading to a brief, perfect wordplay exchange where Dunne says 'both' and Ron completes it with 'Dunne and done'
jokes.explanation: An exceptional piece of wordplay comedy. The exchange is perfectly constructed: the ambiguity of 'Dunne,' Eagleton Ron's economical 'Both,' and Pawnee Ron's button of 'Dunne and done.' The joke works entirely within two men who value brevity — the entire exchange is five words of substance. It's also the setup for the long joke about how these two Rons are initially kindred spirits. Maximum economy, perfect structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, we need to talk about something serious.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, yes. I've been thinking about waffles all morning. Do you think they're better with whipped cream or without? Because I'm leaning towards with, but I could see an argument for without.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, what if you did half and half? Like, whipped cream on one side, nothing on the other? Ann, this could change everything.

jokes.text: I like Ron.
jokes.setup: Ron has just met his Eagleton counterpart and they've exchanged the 'Dunne and done' moment
jokes.punchline: Ron's confessional is a single sentence of approval — his highest possible praise delivered with complete flatness
jokes.explanation: Three words. Ron Swanson's maximum expression of admiration is 'I like Ron.' The economy is perfect — it's the most Ron Swanson possible confessional. The rewatch bonus comes from knowing this opinion will completely collapse. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, did you know that penguins have knees? They do! Look it up! They're just hidden under their feathers. Isn't that incredible? I've been thinking about penguin knees all morning and I completely forgot what we were talking about.

jokes.text: I'm Ragiv from I.T. This is E.R.I.C. / E.R.I.C. is a computer program? / Stands for Eagleton Reservation Information Center. It does all the scheduling in Eagleton.
jokes.setup: Tom has been set up to meet his 'counterpart Eric, who is amazing' — he presumably expects a human rival
jokes.punchline: Eric is a computer program. Tom's job has been automated away in Eagleton.
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection payoff. Leslie said Eric was 'amazing' — and he is, because he's a fully automated system. The callback rewards attentive viewers. The joke also comments on Tom's actual value as a human scheduler in a world with better technology.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I totally understand. You need to do what's best for you. I get it. I support you 100%. Even though you're abandoning me. Abandoning us. After everything we've been through. After I made you my best friend. After I carved out a special place in my heart just for you. A place I can never get back. A place that will now be filled with nothing but regret and a sort of low-level resentment that will probably affect all my future relationships.

jokes.text: You still have a human being in charge of booking tennis courts? What is this, 1990? / I guess that explains the shoulder pads.
jokes.setup: Ragiv condescends about Pawnee using a human scheduler
jokes.punchline: Tom's comeback: 'I guess that explains the shoulder pads' — a sharp insult implying Ragiv is somehow outdated
jokes.explanation: Tom's comeback is somewhat confusing (shoulder pads aren't obviously a Ragiv trait that makes sense) but it functions as a quick character beat showing Tom going on offense. The follow-up visual of Tom staring at his own shoulder pads in the confessional is funnier than the line itself.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh my god, that's so great, Tynnyfer. Blah blah blah, that sounds amazing. Blah blah blah.

jokes.text: How did he notice these? [Tom stares at his own shoulder pads in confessional]
jokes.setup: Tom made fun of Ragiv for 'shoulder pads' — a strange insult
jokes.punchline: Tom's confessional reveals he himself is wearing shoulder pads and is confused how Ragiv noticed — the burn ricocheted
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the shoulder pads joke is much better than the setup. Tom is wearing his own shoulder pads and is baffled that Ragiv spotted them — the insult was an accidental self-own. Perfectly in character for Tom, and the confessional format makes it land beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Like, oh my god, I'm like, so totally into this bonding thing. Like, literally, this is like, the best day ever. I'm like, so blessed right now. Like, I can't even.

jokes.text: I just need to talk some more words into Leslie's face.
jokes.setup: Ann has introduced Evelyn to Leslie and is awkwardly trying to arrange a private conversation
jokes.punchline: 'I just need to talk some more words into Leslie's face' — an oddly clinical description of human conversation that reveals Ann's anxiety about what she needs to say
jokes.explanation: Excellent line. 'Talk some more words into Leslie's face' is a wonderfully strange formulation — it reduces conversation to its physical components while simultaneously conveying Ann's difficulty with what she needs to say. The awkwardness of the phrasing is itself the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Friendship is like a three-legged dog — it's messy, it doesn't make sense, and someone's always getting dragged somewhere they don't want to go.

jokes.text: Pawnee has the very first documented case of mega-diabetes. And the only known occurrence of Lou Gehrig's other disease. We've been written about in textbooks.
jokes.setup: Evelyn notes there wasn't much health work in Eagleton because residents are very healthy
jokes.punchline: Leslie responds with perverse civic pride about Pawnee's record-setting diseases — 'mega-diabetes' and 'Lou Gehrig's other disease,' presenting them as achievements
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Mega-diabetes' is a brilliant coinage — the prefix 'mega' applied to a disease suggests Pawnee's dietary disasters have evolved beyond normal parameters. 'Lou Gehrig's other disease' implies Lou Gehrig had a SECOND disease that Pawnee also discovered, which is darkly absurd. Leslie's civic pride about being written about in textbooks for catastrophic public health failures is perfect character work. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Tynnyfer
dialogue.line: I have two kids. Well, I have two kids now. I used to have three, but I had them surgically removed and combined into two larger, more efficient children.

jokes.text: Nobody can fill your shoes, Ann. With your tiny little doll feet.
jokes.setup: Leslie is being sincere about Ann being irreplaceable
jokes.punchline: She undercuts her own sentiment mid-compliment by adding 'with your tiny little doll feet' — an affectionate but absurdly specific physical detail
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie-and-Ann dynamic — a sincere compliment derailed by a specific physical observation that only a best friend would make. 'Tiny little doll feet' is specific enough to be genuinely funny. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, look at that. It's waffles! Delicious waffles. / Wait. Should we try? Yeah, let's try.
jokes.setup: Ann is trying to tell Leslie something difficult about potentially leaving Pawnee
jokes.punchline: Leslie spots waffles and immediately redirects with complete sincerity — both of them end up eating waffles instead of having the conversation
jokes.explanation: A good Leslie character beat — her love of waffles is a running series gag, and here it functions as a subconscious avoidance mechanism. The joke works because Ann goes along with it, delaying the hard conversation. Character-integrated and situationally earned.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I'm very fond of nuts. Macadamia nuts, Brazil nuts, walnuts... I love all kinds of nuts.

jokes.text: So, if I'm hearing you correctly, you're telling me you're not thinking about leaving Pawnee. / I am thinking about leaving. / Is this one of those classic Ann 'not' jokes? Like, 'I'm leaving Pawnee...not!' / I don't do that. / I was hoping that you had started.
jokes.setup: Ann has just told Leslie she's thinking about leaving
jokes.punchline: Leslie's denial reframes Ann's statement as a joke — specifically a '90s-style 'not' joke — and then reveals she'd been hoping Ann would adopt them
jokes.explanation: Excellent Leslie joke. Her desperate reframing of Ann's announcement as a '90s 'not' joke — a denial so creative it involves reinventing Ann's comedic style — and then the reveal that she'd been hoping Ann would start doing 'not' jokes, is both funny and deeply character-specific. The joke works on three levels: Leslie's denial, Leslie's wishful thinking, and the absurdity of her specific solution.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: A freegan is someone who eats only food that would otherwise be discarded. They dumpster dive for their meals.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: It's actually a very sustainable lifestyle.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: It's disgusting. I once saw a freegan pull a half-eaten rotisserie chicken out of a dumpster behind a grocery store. He inspected it, shrugged, and took a bite.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's... that's not typical.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: He then pulled out a binder labeled 'Chicken Rankings by Dumpster' and made notes.

jokes.text: Do you hear that galloping? / Wha--oh, my--look at that! Joe Biden on a horse shirtless.
jokes.setup: Leslie is being confronted with Ann's news about potentially leaving
jokes.punchline: Leslie is saved by the appearance of Joe Biden riding a horse shirtless — an absurdist real-world intrusion that perfectly serves Leslie's avoidance of the conversation (Joe Biden is a known Leslie hero in the show's universe)
jokes.explanation: A beautifully executed absurdist gag that is perfectly character-integrated. Leslie's obsession with Joe Biden is a well-established series running gag, and a shirtless-horseback Biden appearing at exactly the moment Leslie needs an out is a divine comedy gift. 'Joe Biden on a horse shirtless' is an immediately quotable image. The joke also advances the emotional plot — Leslie's avoidance of Ann's news is externalized as literal magical intervention.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I wear these boots because they're practical. A man needs proper footwear for the work he does. These boots have lasted me fifteen years.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Now, I know what you're thinking — 'Ron, aren't those made of leather?' Yes. Yes they are. And I have no problem with that. A cow gave its life so I could have reliable footwear. That's the natural order.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: What I won't do is wear shoes made from some endangered species. That's not about animal rights — that's about respecting the balance of nature. If you wear a shoe made from a creature that only has six left in the world, you're a fool and a communist.

jokes.text: Uh, I've got a ton of work to do. I'm super busy, so you... can let yourself...
jokes.setup: Ann is waiting for Leslie to say something emotionally real about potentially leaving
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response is to trail off with a dismissal — she can't even complete her own deflection, unable to process the information or say goodbye properly
jokes.explanation: A quieter character beat — Leslie's emotional avoidance expressed through inability to finish a sentence. Functional cringe-comedy, but mostly serves the emotional plot rather than the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, I'll handle Eric. Don't worry about it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm thinking... I'm really considering all the angles here... Okay, here's what we're gonna do.

jokes.text: Look, if Ann wants to leave Pawnee, I get it. I mean, who wants to stay in the greatest town in the world with her best friend and be happy forever when she can abandon her soul sister like an old shoe and move to a garbage city full of jerks. I get it. No hard feelings.
jokes.setup: Leslie is supposed to be processing Ann's potential departure calmly
jokes.punchline: The 'I get it' framework barely conceals escalating devastation — 'garbage city full of jerks,' 'abandon her soul sister like an old shoe' — before returning to 'I get it. No hard feelings.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent confessional rant. The repeating 'I get it' structure is a perfect frame for escalating passive aggression. 'Abandon her soul sister like an old shoe' is a great line — the specific comparison to an old shoe is wonderfully undignified for such a dramatic declaration. 'Garbage city full of jerks' delivers the emotional truth under the 'no hard feelings' veneer. Highly quotable Leslie moment.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I could leave him. I got options.

jokes.text: Sorry for the delay, ladies, I was busy being ambushed by treachery.
jokes.setup: Leslie returns to April and Tynnyfer after processing Ann's news
jokes.punchline: 'I was busy being ambushed by treachery' — Leslie frames a conversation with her best friend as a military betrayal
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable Leslie line. The hyperbolic framing of Ann's conversation as treachery-ambush is perfectly in Leslie's rhetorical register. 'Ambushed by treachery' has the right mock-epic flavor for her character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben saw my new outfit and just said, 'That looks nice.' That looks nice? That's it?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What do you want me to say?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't know, something with more energy! 'Leslie, you look absolutely stunning in that outfit. The way that color brings out your eyes is simply mesmerizing.' But no, I get 'That looks nice.'

jokes.text: Tynny and I have been, like, totally bonding. We've just been like blah blah blah blah blah blah blah! Like, talking, like, so much forever. / It was all so delicious.
jokes.setup: April has been secretly hating Tynnyfer's type, but is presenting to Leslie as if they bonded
jokes.punchline: April's report of their bonding is entirely composed of meaningless filler — 'blah blah blah blah blah' and 'talking so much forever' — which could either be April mocking the conversation or genuinely how she experienced it
jokes.explanation: Works on the ironic level — we know April is mimicking Tynnyfer-speak, but the ambiguity of whether April is mocking or genuinely adapting is character-rich. 'So much forever' is a funny construction.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, what is this? You've signed contracts with every vendor in the city.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes. I have. Because I'm going to need them all for the Harvest Festival.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The Harvest Festival is in three weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know. That's why I've already signed the contracts. If I waited until two weeks before, I'd be behind schedule.

jokes.text: Wow. It's nice to see a friendship blossoming instead of wiling away like a dying turd flower.
jokes.setup: Leslie is commenting on April and Tynnyfer's apparent bond, presumably while still processing Ann's potential departure
jokes.punchline: 'Wiling away like a dying turd flower' — an unexpectedly grotesque metaphor for a friendship fading, delivered in Leslie's typically upbeat register
jokes.explanation: 'Dying turd flower' is an inspired, unexpected coinage. The contrast between Leslie's optimistic delivery and the grotesque specific imagery is the core of the joke. It's also clearly subtext about Ann — the friendship Leslie fears is 'wiling away' is her own. Original metaphor, highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to make the most beautiful cookies with frosting made from... ketchup.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, no.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And mayonnaise swirls!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, please stop.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A little mustard accent for tartness.

jokes.text: We also came up with these nicknames for each other. Slut and Skank.
jokes.setup: Leslie is pleased about April and Tynnyfer's friendship
jokes.punchline: Their chosen nicknames for each other are 'Slut and Skank' — delivered with complete earnestness as terms of endearment
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the breezy delivery — naming each other 'Slut and Skank' as if they're sweet pet names. The shock-to-earnestness ratio works well. It also reflects both characters: April's dark sensibility and Tynnyfer's oblivious enthusiasm.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Mmm, these are... these are really something. The chocolate chips and the anchovies really complement each other.

jokes.text: Well, you know what I think is craze-mazing? Commitment. I'm looking for someone who's in it for the long haul.
jokes.setup: April has used the Eagleton word 'craze-mazing'
jokes.punchline: Leslie co-opts the word to pivot into a speech about commitment — she's using their slang against them to make a point, which is both funny and very Leslie
jokes.explanation: Decent Leslie bit — her co-opting of 'craze-mazing' to deliver a serious civic speech is on-brand. The tonal collision is the joke. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You look great today, Evelyn. I mean, you're almost as pretty as Ann.

jokes.text: Ew, no. I've had so much rejuvenation that I don't think a baby could get out of there if it tried.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Tynnyfer if she has kids, as part of evaluating her commitment to staying
jokes.punchline: Tynnyfer's 'Ew, no' followed by the specific overshare that she's had so much cosmetic work done that childbirth would be physically impossible
jokes.explanation: A great overshare joke with a dark edge. Tynnyfer's explanation that cosmetic 'rejuvenation' has made natural childbirth impossible is both a specific satirical jab at wealthy cosmetic-obsessed culture and a genuinely funny non-sequitur image. The casual breezy delivery amplifies the dark content.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I'm busy. I'm working on a project that connects all the dots between seemingly unrelated things.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Like, did you know that if you take the number of letters in 'Parks and Recreation,' multiply it by the average temperature in Pawnee, and divide it by the number of times I've said 'treat yo self,' you get the exact coordinates of where I buried my time capsule?

jokes.text: I guess we can make a switch to Bermuda grass. It's only 80 cents more per square foot? / What? Gimme gimme gimme. You want me to put Bermuda grass in a continental climate that's a six on beaufort scale? In a park with zero drainage?
jokes.setup: A routine discussion about grass for a park
jokes.punchline: Craig's volcanic eruption of highly specific horticultural knowledge — 'continental climate, beaufort scale six, zero drainage' — delivered with the intensity of someone defending their family's honor
jokes.explanation: Craig's specific professional expertise delivered at maximum emotional intensity is the character's core comic engine. The escalation from mild grass suggestion to meteorological and hydrological objections is well-constructed. 'Beaufort scale' is an unexpected technical term that amplifies the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay everyone, listen up! You're going to be on my team whether you like it or not. Ron, you're in charge of woodworking and scowling. April, I need you to be sarcastic and unhelpful. Tom, just... exist near me and occasionally say something about yourself. Ben, you're my deputy, which means you do exactly what I say and look concerned about budgets. And Donna? Just be Donna. Everyone clear? Great! We're going to make this work if it kills me! Which it won't, because I have a seventeen-step contingency plan!

jokes.text: I want Kentucky bluegrass, I want a 10 percent discount, and I want you to apologize to my best friend Donna!
jokes.setup: Craig has been making technical demands about grass varieties
jokes.punchline: The third demand — 'apologize to my best friend Donna' — arrives as a completely non-sequitur emotional demand alongside the professional ones
jokes.explanation: The rule of three with a devastating swerve. The first two demands are professional (bluegrass, discount), the third is deeply personal (apologize to his best friend Donna). The sudden emotional escalation into friendship loyalty is perfectly Craig — his intensity doesn't distinguish between professional and personal. Highly quotable. One of the episode's best Craig moments.

dialogue.speaker: Tynnyfer
dialogue.line: April, you're like a skinny Mother Teresa.

jokes.text: Is there -- and I'm just guessing here -- some kind of medication that you maybe need a lot of and have taken none of or maybe too much of today?
jokes.setup: Craig has just had his emotional meltdown about Bermuda grass and Donna
jokes.punchline: Donna's perfectly calibrated response — hedged, casual, but precisely targeting Craig's mental state — delivered with total cool
jokes.explanation: Donna's deadpan is perfectly deployed here. The careful hedging ('and I'm just guessing here,' 'maybe...none of or maybe too much of') mirrors the kind of delicate language used around volatile people. The specificity of the construction is funny — she's clearly thought about how to word this.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I decided to prank Jerry by putting a 'kick me' sign on his back. But then I thought, why stop there? I could put a 'punch me' sign. Then a 'stab me' sign. Then I could actually stab him. Not fatally, just like, in the shoulder or something. Then I could go to jail, break out of jail, and stab him again.

jokes.text: Oh, I have a medical condition all right. It's called caring too much! And it's incurable! / Also I have eczema.
jokes.setup: Donna has asked if Craig needs medication — Craig denies he has a problem
jokes.punchline: His 'medical condition' of caring too much, delivered with grandiose drama, is then immediately deflated by the addition 'Also I have eczema' — a real, boring medical condition tacked on as an afterthought
jokes.explanation: Among the episode's very best jokes. The structure is near-perfect: Craig's grandiose declaration 'It's called caring too much! And it's incurable!' is immediately — and completely — deflated by 'Also I have eczema.' The bathos is exquisite. The eczema is a real medical condition that is the exact opposite of dramatic, which makes it the perfect puncture. This joke would land hard in a room and is highly quotable. A strong contender for the episode's highlight.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have decided to declare myself Parks Director for life. All decisions will be made by me, and me alone. Anyone who disagrees will be reassigned to the gravel pit. Also, I'm making it illegal to eat lunch at your desk. Punishable by exile.

jokes.text: I'm a yoga nut. And I'm a nut nut. They make delicious milks, man.
jokes.setup: Eagleton Ron is listing his interests, mirroring Pawnee Ron's presumed preferences
jokes.punchline: 'I'm a nut nut' — an immediate wordplay on 'yoga nut' that pivots to literal nut enthusiasm, landing on 'They make delicious milks, man'
jokes.explanation: The wordplay transition from 'yoga nut' to 'nut nut' is clever, and 'They make delicious milks, man' is a funny, characterful landing point. The Eagleton Ron character is doing effective work as the dark reflection of Pawnee Ron — every value flipped to its hippie-wellness opposite.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, I'm going to give you some advice. You need to treat your friendship with Ann like a government budget. You're spending money you don't have, and it's only going to end badly. Cut her loose.

jokes.text: And I'm a vegan, of course. Slowly working toward full freegan-vegan. / What in God's name is freegan-vegan? / You only eat vegetables that have been thrown out in people's dumpsters.
jokes.setup: Eagleton Ron lists his dietary practices; Pawnee Ron is increasingly alarmed
jokes.punchline: Freegan-vegan — eating only dumpster-discarded vegetables — is the logical extreme of Eagleton Ron's philosophy, and lands as a perfect absurdist escalation
jokes.explanation: A great conceptual joke. 'Freegan-vegan' is a real portmanteau (freeganism is real) but applied to Eagleton Ron's character it becomes a perfect absurdist endpoint. Ron Swanson's horror at someone eating dumpster vegetables is the ideal straight-man reaction — he eats entire animals but finds dumpster lettuce unconscionable. Strong character contrast comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Friendship is two people using each other to avoid loneliness. When it stops being mutually beneficial, one or both of you will leave. It's not personal; it's just human nature. I have three best friends and I trust none of them.

jokes.text: What is on your foot, sir? / My trusty sandals. I believe a man's feet should remain uncaged. / Same goes for all chickens.
jokes.setup: Ron notices something about Eagleton Ron's footwear and asks
jokes.punchline: Eagleton Ron's philosophical response about uncaged feet segues immediately into animal rights advocacy — 'Same goes for all chickens' — connecting his sandal philosophy to his veganism in one absurd leap
jokes.explanation: Excellent construction. The pivot from 'feet should remain uncaged' to 'same goes for all chickens' is a genuinely funny logical connection — Eagleton Ron applies his sandal philosophy to poultry liberation with complete seriousness. 'Same goes for all chickens' is an instantly quotable line. The joke accelerates Pawnee Ron's disillusionment effectively.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I believe that all government is a waste of taxpayer money. Except for national defense, and maybe... roads.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ron, that's actually... kind of reasonable?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Don't sound so surprised. I have principles.

jokes.text: I no longer like Ron.
jokes.setup: Pawnee Ron has been learning more and more that Eagleton Ron is his philosophical opposite
jokes.punchline: Ron's confessional is again a single sentence — the perfect reversal of 'I like Ron' — same structure, opposite conclusion
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes precisely because of its structural callback. The mirror image of 'I like Ron' delivered in identical format — flat, three words, single confessional — is a perfect comedic callback. The journey from approval to disapproval in one beat captures everything about Ron's character: his economy with words, his absolute standards, his willingness to reverse completely. Structurally the best callback in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So I went to IT, right? And I told them my computer was broken. They said they'd replace it, but it would take two weeks. Two weeks! So I said, 'You know what? I'm going to fight for this. I'm going to march back to that office every single day until you give me a new computer.' And you know what happened? They gave me a new computer the next day.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm basically a war hero now.

jokes.text: But there's one thing no man or machine can beat Tom Haverford at — talking mad trash till I get what I want.
jokes.setup: Tom has just learned his job has been automated by E.R.I.C.
jokes.punchline: Tom's response is to identify his unique value proposition: strategic trash-talking. The confidence with which he states this as his professional superpower is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Good Tom moment — 'talking mad trash till I get what I want' as a professional skill is both hilarious and accurate to the character. The setup (losing to a computer program) makes the confidence funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: My DVR is like a pregnancy. It started out as something I was excited about, but now I'm just terrified and I don't know how it's going to end.

jokes.text: This guy Eric is a disaster. / What do you mean? / Just a bad attitude. 'Oh, I hate this place. Get me out here.' That kind of thing. And unreliable. And racist. / I think he may have even been to jail. Although, you know, maybe those are just regular face tattoos.
jokes.setup: Tom claims to be sabotaging Eric to protect his job — but Eric is a computer program, making all of this impossible
jokes.punchline: Tom's fabricated complaints escalate from 'bad attitude' to 'racist' to 'maybe been to jail' to 'maybe those are just regular face tattoos' — increasingly absurd lies about a software program
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation joke that works on two levels: (1) Tom's accelerating lies are funny on their own, and (2) the audience knows he's describing a computer program, making 'racist' and 'face tattoos' even funnier. 'Maybe those are just regular face tattoos' as a charitable hedge about a software program is inspired. The rewatch bonus is high because rewatchers know E.R.I.C.'s nature from the start.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You know, Chris, I was thinking about our time in the accounting department together.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Yeah, those were some dark days.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The darkest. I remember thinking it was because of the spreadsheets, the budget cuts, the endless reports.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Right, the work was soul-crushing.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But I just realized something. It wasn't the work that made us sad.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We were lonely. We were just two guys in a room full of numbers, with no one to share it with.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Oh man. That's... actually really sad.

jokes.text: 400 Segway scooters. Sell 'em. They're gone. / You had six full-time baristas on the payroll. The baristas are gone. As are the masseurs. And the full-time barista who provided coffee for the masseurs.
jokes.setup: Ben and Chris are auditing Eagleton's assets
jokes.punchline: The escalating absurdity of Eagleton's government payroll: 400 Segways, professional masseurs, and a dedicated barista whose entire job was making coffee for the other masseurs
jokes.explanation: The list comedy works well here. The escalation from absurd (400 Segways) to specific-absurd (masseurs) to meta-absurd (a barista who only makes coffee for the masseurs) is perfectly structured. The final item in the list is the funniest because it's a support staff position for a support staff position.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm looking for something healthy to eat. Do you have any quinoa bowls?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: We have a kale salad.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Perfect. What's in it?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Kale, bacon, ranch dressing, and deep fried croutons.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: How much bacon?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: A lot.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'll have the burger.

jokes.text: It is excellent having the old band back together again. You know what? This calls for some celebratory lunges. One... two...
jokes.setup: Chris and Ben are enjoying working together again while eliminating jobs
jokes.punchline: Chris's celebration of firing people takes the form of 'celebratory lunges' — his physical fitness enthusiasm is completely tone-deaf to the context of mass unemployment
jokes.explanation: Chris's physical fitness enthusiasm deployed in the wrong context is a reliable character joke. 'Celebratory lunges' is a great specific detail — not pushups, not jumping jacks, specifically lunges — which feels very Chris.

jokes.text: I mean, your job is secure, of course. You're basically the glue of this department. / But I think Craig's gonna have to go. / No, you should keep him. He's crazy intense, but I've never met anyone who cares more about this job. / Uh, Donna, I'm right here.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Donna discuss staffing cuts; Craig is present
jokes.punchline: Craig's quiet, wounded 'Uh, Donna, I'm right here' after Donna advocates for him while treating him as absent
jokes.explanation: A classic cringe beat — someone being discussed as if absent when they're present. The joke is that Donna is defending Craig but can't be bothered to include him in the conversation. Functional; Craig's deflated 'I'm right here' is appropriately pathetic.

jokes.text: No joke. He might care more than you. Honestly, if I had to choose between him and me, I'd choose him.
jokes.setup: Donna has been told her own job is secure; she's now advocating for Craig over herself
jokes.punchline: Donna volunteering herself for elimination in favor of someone she just met — 'if I had to choose between him and me, I'd choose him' — delivered with perfect Donna practicality
jokes.explanation: Donna's cool practicality in self-nominating for elimination is funny in its casualness. The joke is how quickly she's assessed Craig's value and decided he outranks her — with no apparent emotional distress.

jokes.text: You know, I got the condo in Seattle, the fiancé in Denver. / Huh? / It won't last.
jokes.setup: Donna casually mentions she could retire and lists reasons she'd be fine
jokes.punchline: She mentions a fiancé in Denver as a reason she'd be okay — then pre-emptively dismisses him: 'It won't last.'
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical character joke. Donna mentions a fiancé as a positive — then immediately dismisses him as a future fact in two words. 'It won't last.' captures Donna's unsentimental self-assurance perfectly. The 'Huh?' reaction beat before it makes it land harder. Pure character comedy at its best.

jokes.text: What? Even Larry wants out? What the hell is happening here? Does everybody think that running a town is just some game where people can come and go as they please?
jokes.setup: After Ann, Donna, and now Larry all express willingness to leave, Leslie reaches critical mass
jokes.punchline: Leslie's outrage framing of staff turnover as existential betrayal — 'does everybody think running a town is just some GAME?' — the hyperbole is the joke
jokes.explanation: Competent Leslie frustration moment. The line about 'a game where people can come and go as they please' is solid but not her funniest phrasing. More emotional plot engine than pure comedy.

jokes.text: I'll tell you what's not fair. I'm gonna have to watch the Oscars with Ben alone this year. Last year, don't you remember Angelina Jolie and the leg dress moment? He had, and I quote, 'no comment.'
jokes.setup: Ann is telling Leslie she's being unfair; Leslie is supposed to be defending her position about town loyalty
jokes.punchline: Leslie pivots to the real injustice: Ben's insufficient reaction to the Angelina Jolie leg dress moment at the Oscars — the deeply personal, specific, and completely disproportionate grievance
jokes.explanation: Excellent Leslie joke. The pivot from civic governance to Oscar night watch parties is a perfect tonal mismatch. The specific detail — Ben had 'no comment' on the Angelina leg dress — is both very Leslie (she demands extreme reactions to pop culture moments) and very funny as the actual injustice she can't let go of. 'And I quote: no comment' is a great construction. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: How can you not have an extreme reaction about a dress like that? It just doesn't make any sense!
jokes.setup: Leslie is continuing her Oscars grievance
jokes.punchline: Leslie's genuine incomprehension that someone could be unmoved by a red carpet fashion moment — presented as a serious epistemological failure
jokes.explanation: Extension of the previous joke — works better as part of the bit than standalone. The follow-through diminishes slightly from the initial pivot.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, Ann. I can't understand you. You've developed some accent from that new town you might move to!
jokes.setup: Ann is trying to talk Leslie through her reaction
jokes.punchline: Leslie pretends she literally cannot understand Ann's accent from a hypothetical future city she hasn't moved to yet
jokes.explanation: A great Leslie evasion — pre-emptively alienating Ann by pretending she's already foreign. The absurdity of Ann having acquired an accent from a city she hasn't moved to yet is perfect Leslie logic. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: I'm just trying to stop time with legally-binding friendship contracts. What part of that do you not understand?
jokes.setup: Ben has asked why Leslie is giving everyone 50-year contracts
jokes.punchline: Leslie's completely earnest description of her goal — 'stop time with legally-binding friendship contracts' — delivered as if this is a perfectly reasonable thing to explain
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest Leslie lines. 'Stop time with legally-binding friendship contracts' is a perfect crystallization of Leslie Knope — her bureaucratic instincts deployed in service of emotional control, and her total earnestness about it. The follow-up 'What part of that do you not understand?' treats this as a reasonable plan that others are simply failing to comprehend. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific. Could only be Leslie.

jokes.text: Basic boilerplate language, 50-year commitment, blah, blah, blah.
jokes.setup: Leslie presents 50-year employment/friendship contracts she drafted to prevent people from leaving.
jokes.punchline: 'Blah blah blah' used to minimize a 50-year legal commitment as if it's a minor detail. Her complete comfort with how extreme this is makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: The 50-year commitment as 'boilerplate' is a great character joke. Leslie's institutional thoroughness applied to personal relationships is a core comedy engine for her character. 'Blah blah blah' is the right dismissive delivery for something this extreme.

jokes.text: I think you need a spa day, Les. / Fine! You only have to work here until I'm dead! Is that better?
jokes.setup: Ann tries to de-escalate Leslie's contract demands
jokes.punchline: Leslie's furious compromise — reducing the 50-year contract to 'until I'm dead' — presents her mortality as a concession
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation. 'You only have to work here until I'm dead! Is that better?' is Leslie offering her own death as a contractual endpoint — a concession that is simultaneously generous (no more 50 years) and completely insane. 'Is that better?' as a genuine check-in about whether this compromise is satisfactory is the button that makes it land.

jokes.text: What in the name of all that is holy is that smell? / Yerba matte tea. Sweetened with stevia. It's an all-natural plant extract. / Shut your damn mouth. / No need to curse. / There most certainly is.
jokes.setup: Ron detects an unusual smell from Eagleton Ron
jokes.punchline: Eagleton Ron's herbal tea triggers Ron's visceral disgust — 'Shut your damn mouth' — followed by a brief exchange where Eagleton Ron's gentleness is met with Ron's insistence that there absolutely is a need to curse
jokes.explanation: The Ron vs. Eagleton Ron contrast is the episode's sustained comedic engine, and this exchange is well-executed. 'There most certainly is [a need to curse]' is a great Ron button. The gentle/ferocious contrast between the two Rons is at its sharpest here.

jokes.text: And take it personally.
jokes.setup: Ron has separated Eagleton and Pawnee employees, telling Pawnee staff to sit at their desks
jokes.punchline: The unexpected addendum — 'And take it personally' — turning a routine instruction into an emotional directive
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum comedy. Ron telling his Pawnee staff to sit at their desks 'and take it personally' is perfectly Ron — authoritative, unexpectedly emotive, and completely deadpan. It validates Pawnee pride while creating comic escalation of the Eagleton/Pawnee rivalry. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: However, I did not have yellow frosting, so I had to use mustard. But do not worry. I put tons of sugar on them, so it will even it out. / Mmm! Sugar mustard.
jokes.setup: Leslie presents unity cookies with town colors — but reveals the yellow is mustard
jokes.punchline: 'Sugar mustard' — a recipient's genuine positive reaction to what is objectively a horrible food combination, because Leslie's earnest belief that sugar fixes everything is contagious
jokes.explanation: The mustard cookie bit is a great Leslie joke — her confidence that sugar will fix mustard frosting is entirely in character, and someone actually enthusiastically eating one ('Mmm! Sugar mustard') is a funny beat. 'Sugar mustard' as a satisfied label for a terrible thing is quotable.

jokes.text: That's awful kind of you, Leslie, but I'm afraid those are a little too sweet for me. I unhooked from that big sugar train over 30 years ago.
jokes.setup: Leslie offers her mustard/sugar cookies as a unity gesture
jokes.punchline: 'That big sugar train' — Eagleton Ron's folksy metaphor for sugar addiction, framing his dietary choice as a recovery narrative with the flavor of a 12-step program
jokes.explanation: 'The big sugar train' is a nicely folksy and unexpected metaphor. Eagleton Ron declining the cookies with the language of a reformed addict treating sugar as his former substance of choice is both character-specific and original.

jokes.text: So, what's your story, new Ann? You're kind of pretty. I mean, you're not 'Ann' pretty, but you have potential. / Thank you, but I-I don't work in this department. / Shut your kind of pretty mouth and, uh, eat a mustard cookie.
jokes.setup: Leslie encounters Evelyn, Ann's health department counterpart
jokes.punchline: 'You're not Ann pretty' — Leslie's compliment that Evelyn is pretty is immediately qualified as not reaching Ann's tier — and then 'Shut your kind of pretty mouth and eat a mustard cookie' echoes the earlier compliment structure in an order
jokes.explanation: Excellent Leslie joke about Ann. 'You're not Ann pretty' establishes Ann as the gold standard of prettiness in Leslie's hierarchy, which is both sweet and funny. The callback of 'shut your kind of pretty mouth' reusing the compliment as a command is well-constructed. Strong character integration — this is entirely about Leslie's adoration of Ann.

jokes.text: Okay, so let's chit-chat, huh? Let's get to know each other and then become familiar best friends.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to fast-track friendship with Eagletonians to replace her departing friends
jokes.punchline: 'Let's get to know each other and then become familiar best friends' — the bureaucratic scheduling of friendship, with 'familiar' as a qualification level
jokes.explanation: A good Leslie beat — the agenda-driven approach to spontaneous friendship. 'Become familiar best friends' as a staged process is the kind of over-organized Leslie-speak that characterizes her.

jokes.text: I don't have time for this. I'm halfway through designing a bamboo gazebo as a tribute to the founders of Motown.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to force-bond everyone
jokes.punchline: Craig's dismissal reveals he's in the middle of an extremely specific and unusual project — a bamboo gazebo tribute to Motown founders — which is both Craig-intense and completely unexpected
jokes.explanation: Excellent Craig absurdism. A bamboo gazebo honoring Motown founders is the precise kind of intensely specific, culturally enthusiastic, oddly specific passion project that Craig would be halfway through. The specificity ('halfway through,' 'bamboo,' 'founders of Motown') makes it feel like an actual Craig project rather than a random non-sequitur.

jokes.text: That's so Craig. / Oh, Craig! We have fun, don't we?
jokes.setup: Craig makes an intense remark; Leslie reacts
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'That's so Craig' and 'Oh, Craig!' are deliberately performing the warmth and in-jokes of established friendship — she's manufacturing the feeling of having a history with someone she just met
jokes.explanation: A good meta-joke about Leslie manufacturing retroactive friendship. 'That's so Craig' implies a deep knowledge of Craig that Leslie absolutely does not have yet, and 'We have fun, don't we?' invites Craig to confirm a history that doesn't exist. Character-specific and self-aware.

jokes.text: Do you guys remember when this all started and I came in here with the cookies, and then Craig said something so Craig and we all laughed, and we were like, 'Craig!'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to create a nostalgia for events that happened minutes ago
jokes.punchline: Leslie is narrating the meeting they are currently in as if it's an old memory — 'remember when this all started?' — manufacturing shared history in real time
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Leslie narrating the current meeting as if it's already a cherished memory — 'remember when this all started and I came in here with the cookies' — while still in that moment is a brilliant, deeply Leslie-specific comedic concept. The fake-nostalgic 'we were like Craig!' as a recreated group laugh is exquisite. This joke could only happen on Parks and Recreation with this character.

jokes.text: Do you think it would be weird if we held hands? / Probably. / This way, please.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been forcing group bonding; now she floats the idea of holding hands
jokes.punchline: Ron's interruption with 'This way, please' — overriding Leslie's hand-holding initiative with complete authority and zero comment on the weirdness of her request
jokes.explanation: Ron's interruption is perfectly timed. He doesn't address the hand-holding question — he simply overrides it with an instruction. The economy of his interjection is very Ron. Works as a relief-valve from Leslie's escalating friendship mania.

jokes.text: Excuse me, Ron, I am talking to my best friends. / Let me go! Best friends, attack Ron!
jokes.setup: Ron has physically redirected Leslie away from her forced bonding session
jokes.punchline: Leslie calling on her new 'best friends' (people she met today) to physically attack Ron — deployed with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: 'Best friends, attack Ron!' is a great line — Leslie commanding people she met hours ago to assault her colleague as a test of loyalty. The phrase has the right mix of desperation and absurdity.

jokes.text: Ben, it has been an honor watching you work today. It's been like watching Leonardo work. Da Vinci or DiCaprio. You're that good.
jokes.setup: Chris is complimenting Ben on his auditing work
jokes.punchline: Chris clarifies 'Leonardo' could be Da Vinci or DiCaprio — and the clarification is funnier than the compliment, because comparing Ben to a working accountant to DiCaprio is absurd
jokes.explanation: The 'Da Vinci or DiCaprio' hedge is the joke — Chris's generous uncertainty about which Leonardo is the higher compliment reveals that he considers them equally great. Very Chris in its earnest hyperbole.

jokes.text: I know who I'm gonna use to calculate tax and tip. / Me?
jokes.setup: Ben suggests celebrating dinner 'like the old days'
jokes.punchline: Ben reveals he's excited about using Chris to calculate tax and tip — a deeply unglamorous use of what he just described as Leonardo-level brilliance
jokes.explanation: A good accounting-nerd joke. Ben's idea of celebrating is using Chris's mental math for a dinner bill. The 'Me?' — Chris's genuinely pleased reaction — makes it land. The humor is in the modest scope of Ben's excitement.

jokes.text: You don't want this job. Seriously, this place is the pits. It's like, if you worked here, you'd be like, 'Ugh!' And Leslie would be like, 'Blah, blah, blah.' And you'd be like, 'Uh...'
jokes.setup: April and Tynnyfer have been bonding — now April is apparently giving Tynnyfer career advice
jokes.punchline: April's anti-job pitch is delivered in their shared Tynnyfer-speak, with Leslie reduced to 'Blah, blah, blah' — April's loyalty to Pawnee is expressed through strategic reverse psychology using Tynnyfer's own language
jokes.explanation: A quietly excellent April moment. She has entirely adopted Tynnyfer's speech patterns to strategically push her away from the job — using the enemy's language as a weapon. Leslie reduced to 'Blah, blah, blah' is also a funny callback to April's own earlier description of their bonding. The loyalty underneath April's nihilist facade is well-earned.

jokes.text: Okay, can I say something? Right now, I totally think that you're right, and I had been thinking about going someplace warm while my husband is in jail.
jokes.setup: Tynnyfer appears to be agreeing with April that the job isn't right for her
jokes.punchline: The sudden revelation — 'while my husband is in jail' — delivered as casually as any of the previous wellness chat
jokes.explanation: A great overshare drop. The casual insertion of 'while my husband is in jail' into a chirpy conversation is a perfect Tynnyfer move — for her, this is just one more life circumstance delivered in the same register as spinning class recommendations. The dark detail amplifies her oblivious-wellness persona.

jokes.text: You should totally stay at my house in Miami. / What? / I'm serious. Come by anytime. Just let yourself in. The gate kind of jams sometimes, but you can just jump it.
jokes.setup: April is being unusually generous, offering her Miami house to Tynnyfer
jokes.punchline: It's not April's house — as revealed momentarily. The 'gate kind of jams but you can jump it' detail is a specific false sincerity that makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: The gate detail ('kind of jams, but you can just jump it') is what elevates this — it's the level of specificity that makes April sound like she actually owns this house. The reveal that it's Dwayne Wade's house makes the entire sequence funnier on rewatch.

jokes.text: You are so amazing right now. You're like skinny Mother Theresa.
jokes.setup: April has offered Tynnyfer a house in Miami
jokes.punchline: 'Skinny Mother Theresa' — Tynnyfer's highest compliment combines saintly altruism with a body type qualifier, which reveals everything about her value system
jokes.explanation: 'Skinny Mother Theresa' is an excellent coinage. The joke is in the qualifier — for Tynnyfer, even a saint requires a body-conscious modifier to be the highest compliment. It's both a funny line and a sharp character revelation that her world filters everything through appearance. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: It's Dwayne Wade's house. I got his address off the Internet. I really hope he's there when she walks in and he throws a basketball at her head.
jokes.setup: April has just generously offered Tynnyfer 'her' house in Miami
jokes.punchline: April's confessional reveals she gave Tynnyfer Dwayne Wade's home address from the internet and specifically hopes he beans her with a basketball
jokes.explanation: The episode's funniest moment. April's entire 'generous' Miami house offer was actually setting up an NBA star to accidentally assault someone with a basketball. The construction is immaculate: the warmth of the setup (April bonding with Tynnyfer, offering her house), the reveal (it's Dwayne Wade's address from the internet), and the specific, gleeful hope that 'he throws a basketball at her head.' It's dark, it's April, it's perfectly structured, and 'he throws a basketball at her head' is an image that will stay with the audience. Purely April Ludgate. Among the best April jokes in the series.

jokes.text: Nice, Ron? Edible arrangements are nice. This is volcanically hot betrayal!
jokes.setup: Ron has responded to Ann's potential departure with 'Well, that's nice.'
jokes.punchline: Leslie's furious correction — 'Edible arrangements are nice. This is volcanically hot betrayal!' — the contrast between the mundanity of Edible Arrangements and 'volcanically hot betrayal' as a temperature metaphor
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout lines. 'Edible arrangements are nice' as the baseline for 'nice' is a perfectly chosen reference — Edible Arrangements are inoffensive, generic gift items that exist in a zone of pleasant mediocrity. Contrasting that with 'volcanically hot betrayal' is both conceptually original and linguistically excellent. The temperature escalation (nice vs. volcanically hot) is also well-observed. Highly quotable, strong character integration.

jokes.text: She is my best friend! She's thinking about leaving, just like that! And she wants to 'talk to me' about it? It's like, I don't even know what to say.
jokes.setup: Leslie is ranting about Ann's potential departure
jokes.punchline: Leslie's outrage at Ann wanting to 'talk to her' about it — the air-quotes around 'talk to me' treating basic communication as a further offense
jokes.explanation: Functional Leslie rant moment. The irony of Leslie saying she doesn't know what to say while saying plenty is noted, but this is more emotional plot than pure comedy.

jokes.text: That you love her and you understand that it's her life, and geography will never change your feelings. / Whatever. I don't even need her. I've got Tynnyfer now, and Craig, and Eric, the racist drug dealer who I've yet to meet.
jokes.setup: Ron offers Leslie the emotionally correct thing to say to Ann; Leslie rejects it
jokes.punchline: Leslie's replacement friends list ends with 'Eric, the racist drug dealer who I've yet to meet' — a callback to Tom's fabricated description, which Leslie has apparently accepted as fact
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback. Leslie has taken Tom's entirely made-up description of Eric ('racist drug dealer') as accurate and is now including him in her replacement friend group despite never having met him. The qualifier 'who I've yet to meet' is perfect — she's already formed strong opinions. The joke rewards those paying attention to Tom's earlier scene.

jokes.text: You can't force friendship, Leslie. It takes time. I once thought I had a friend. Then it turned out he was the single worst person I have ever met.
jokes.setup: Ron is counseling Leslie about forced friendship
jokes.punchline: Ron's cautionary tale about friendship — a person who turned out to be 'the single worst person I have ever met' — delivered with Ron's characteristic economy as if this is a settled matter
jokes.explanation: A good Ron confessional that sets up the Eagleton Ron ending. His story about the 'single worst person I have ever met' — delivered with absolute finality, clearly about someone specific — is a great Ron beat. The rewatch bonus is that we know he's about to experience this again.

jokes.text: I agree with Ron, Leslie. It's like Moz once said, 'Hold on to your friends.' / Morrissey. The Smiths. / You don't know Meat Is Murder? It's one of the best songs ever written about industrialized beef consumption.
jokes.setup: Eagleton Ron quotes Morrissey to support Ron's point
jokes.punchline: Eagleton Ron describes 'Meat Is Murder' (a song about animal rights) as 'one of the best songs ever written about industrialized beef consumption' — framing a pro-vegetarian anthem entirely through the lens of its subject matter
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist joke. Describing a landmark animal rights album as 'one of the best songs about industrialized beef consumption' — entirely neutral on whether that's good or bad — is a nicely understated reframing that captures Eagleton Ron's earnest but slightly deranged worldview.

jokes.text: Okay, Eagleton Ron. I think it might be time for you to go. This Ron has the position pretty much locked up.
jokes.setup: Eagleton Ron continues to horrify Pawnee Ron
jokes.punchline: Leslie dismissing Eagleton Ron with the same bureaucratic matter-of-factness as a job rejection while he's still in the room
jokes.explanation: Functional dismissal beat. Leslie applying HR language to the firing of Eagleton Ron works in context. Not especially inventive but moves the plot along.

jokes.text: Fair enough. I should have seen it. Taurus and Capricorns never mix, do they?
jokes.setup: Eagleton Ron is being let go gracefully
jokes.punchline: He blames his firing on astrological incompatibility — 'Taurus and Capricorns never mix' — treating zodiac signs as a reasonable HR explanation
jokes.explanation: A nicely placed character button for Eagleton Ron. His astrological explanation for professional incompatibility is very much his character — finding spiritual/mystical frameworks for practical realities. Good economy.

jokes.text: Just remember, Ron. Giving in to hate is like drinking saltwater. The thirst only grows worse.
jokes.setup: Eagleton Ron is departing; he offers parting wisdom
jokes.punchline: The pseudo-profound fortune-cookie wisdom, delivered with complete earnestness as a final gift to his nemesis
